name: Zoe Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day in your life now, and what your working life was like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm up early with the radio, then I head to the repair café at the library, where I fix toasters, lamps and kids' bikes for free. Back home I work in my shed on reclaimed oak, making small tables I sell at the Saturday market. I use an AI helper every day for cut lists and for talking through tricky joints. I was a joiner for forty-two years, mostly kitchens and staircases for a firm in Millbrook, until I retired at sixty-one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you like most about your craft, and what's it like to be doing it now just for yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I loved the puzzle of fitting wood to a house that's never quite square. The firm got bought by a bigger one in my last years and the new bosses wanted everything faster and cheaper. I'm divorced and live alone in a one-bedroom flat I own outright, but the pension is small and the savings tiny, so the tables bring in the little extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, good, and about time somebody was honest. I use these tools every day and they're handy but they're not magic. I'd tell people at the café that the hype was always bigger than the thing, and that a good helper still needs a person who knows what a straight board looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, privately, not much changes. The AI keeps helping me with my cut lists, and the pension keeps being small. My worry is the money, not the tech. The flat is mine, but the roof needs doing in a couple of years and that's about 4,000 I haven't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep making tables, maybe push to sell two a month instead of one. I'd start taking small commissions, like shelves for neighbours, using the AI to quote materials fast. I'd keep the repair café on Wednesdays and Saturdays. And I'd ask the council about the roof grant for older owners before the roof really goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, a bit unexciting. I'm a curious person, and I'd have liked something wilder. But my money doesn't have a safety net, so boring is just right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a roof that needs doing. What's the plan if the grant doesn't come through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a roof or boiler bill came in, my first cut would be the market stall fees and the van hire. That'd hurt because the market is where I meet people. Then I'd cancel the library fund donations, small as they are. I wouldn't cut the heating, never again after the cold winter of 2019.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the AI helper on a typical day, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think what's useful stays useful. A tool that does routine tasks is just a faster hand plane. But my daughter Imogen, who teaches in the city, says her school is trialling it for marking, and she's a bit nervous. I'd say it's nice to have help but don't give it the final say.

say: I'd say the **hype** was always bigger than the thing, and it still needs a person who knows a straight board.
I'd say it's a handy **tool**, not magic.
think: My real worry is **money**: the roof needs about 4,000 I haven't got.
Nothing changes for me, and that's **fine** with no safety net.
do: Sell **two tables** a month instead of one at the Saturday market.
Take small **commissions** like neighbours' shelves, quoting materials quickly with the AI.
Apply for the council's **roof grant** for older owners.
feel: It feels **unexciting**, but boring is right when there's no safety net.
S0.quote: A tool that does routine tasks is just a faster hand plane.
fieldNote: Adaptive and curious, yet still held back by a **thin cushion** and a future roof bill.
Uses AI daily for practical jobs, not as a belief.
Tables and shelves are her small income.

steps.text: Sell two tables a month at the Saturday market

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already half here. I'd tell the folks at the café and online that if you're older, learn the basics now, because it's easier than you'd think and it helps with forms, quotes and calls. And I'd say the companies owning these tools should pay a share to everybody, because we all fed them our words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it opens things up. A desk job is the first to go, but joinery is hands-on, so robots arrive slowly in my field. And I can use the AI to run a one-woman business: invoices, photos, listings. I could make maybe 300 extra a month if I'm good. But my daughter's school and her friends' offices will feel it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an online shop with product photos and let the AI write the descriptions. I'd learn about 3D design tools to show customers what a custom shelf looks like. I'd teach a Saturday class at the library, 'AI for older people', because I've got the patience. And I'd save the extra 300 a month for the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel excited and a bit guilty. It's good for me, but I know others will lose out. It's like being on the right side of a flood, grateful and uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel on the right side of a flood. Who are you thinking of on the wrong side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Imogen to keep her teaching job but learn how to work with the tools, so she can be the one who decides what the kids need. And I'd tell her not to take her pension for granted. I'd show her the shed and the shop, and say, look, you could do this if school goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the Saturday class look like, and who would come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I didn't have the roof to worry about, I'd be happy. The tech isn't my problem. The problem is the 4,000 and a pension of 1,300 a month. If prices jump because everything shifts, then I'd be in trouble regardless of how clever I am.

say: I'd tell older folks to learn the **basics** now, since it's easier than you'd think.
I'd say the firms owning these tools should pay a **share** to everybody.
think: Joinery is **hands-on**, so robots come slowly, and AI could help me run a one-woman business.
I could make maybe **300 extra** a month if I do it well.
do: Set up an **online shop** with product photos and AI-written descriptions.
Run a Saturday **library class** called AI for older people.
Save the extra 300 a month for the **roof**.
feel: I feel **excited** and guilty, like being on the right side of a flood.
S1.quote: The tech isn't my problem. The problem is the 4,000 and a pension of 1,300 a month.
fieldNote: Sees **opportunity** in AI because she works with her hands.
Guilt toward others who will lose desk jobs.
Her actual pressure is the roof bill and pension size.

steps.text: Open an online shop for custom shelves and tables
Teach a Saturday AI class for older people at the library
Save the extra 300 a month for the roof
Show my daughter Imogen my shed as a back-up plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, right, let's slow down and look at who benefits. Two years is a sprint. I'd be on every forum and at the council saying the same thing, the owners of these systems have to pay into a common fund, like a dividend. I'd even sign up for any citizen assembly they run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm more uneasy than excited. The tools I use will become so good that the market for handmade tables might change, either up or down. People may crave handmade, or they may just print everything. And I have no cushion. If prices go wild, a pension of 1,300 isn't enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any money I can and fix the roof right now, even if it means a loan, because two years from now repairs may cost double. I'd stock up on wood and tools while they are cheap. I'd list every table I can make, and I'd try to sell to people who value handmade. And I'd put 30 a week aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing at the top of a ski slope, thrilled and terrified. I'm curious by nature, so part of me wants to see it. The other part knows I'm sixty-four with little in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you want to fix the roof right now, rather than wait and see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, the thinking work goes first, so the paper side of my world changes. Hands-on and robots come in 2031. So I've got five years of being a person with hands in a world of thinking machines. That could be good, if I'm smart. But I can't be smart about the roof in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd list every table you can make. What would your market look like if everyone could print furniture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Imogen to buy a bit of land or a tool kit, something real, if she can. I don't know if it's good advice, but I'd rather my daughter had a hammer and a patch of soil than only a certificate. I'd tell her that over a good dinner, not on the phone.

I'd say two years is a **sprint** and we need to look at who benefits.
think: I'm more **uneasy** than excited, since handmade tables might gain or lose value.

do: Fix the **roof** now, even with a loan, before repairs cost double.
Stock up on **wood and tools** while they're cheap.
feel: I feel **thrilled** and terrified, like standing at the top of a ski slope.
S2.quote: I'd rather my daughter had a hammer and a patch of soil than only a certificate.
fieldNote: A curious person who still sees the **money risk**.
Her stable, hands-on skills give five years of cover, but not for the pension itself.
Prefers prompt, concrete action, with a loan as her answer.

steps.text: Take a small loan to fix the roof now
Put 30 a week aside in a savings account
Join a citizen assembly or council meeting on a common AI dividend
Tell my daughter Imogen to get real tools and land

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a decent run. I'd say let's use it, build the rules and the training, and make sure older people aren't forgotten. I'd tell the library to run more classes. I'd push the council on a local plan, a simple one: cheap training and a food bank that's reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel pretty okay. I'm sixty-four now, so I'd be sixty-nine, and my body's still in good shape. I'd have time to sell more tables, save for the roof, and learn the tools that come next. The hard part is the pension, because I'd still be on 1,300 and prices could creep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fix the roof within the first year, using a small loan and savings. I'd start a proper workshop in the shed where I take on a young apprentice, someone who wants hands-on skills, because those last longer. I'd also learn the next AI tools as they come, because I like it, and I'd keep the repair café going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a good, brisk challenge. I'm a bit tense, but I enjoy a puzzle. I'd rather know what's coming than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you find and pay for an apprentice on a pension like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The five years change what I do with the apprentice. If I had only two, I'd be in survival mode. With five I could pass on the craft and perhaps earn a bit from teaching. It also gives time for my daughter to plan her next step if teaching gets shaken up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your daughter's next step be if teaching changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to people who are scared, find what you like doing with your hands or with people, and get good at it. The machines can write the invoice, but they can't tell you which board has a hidden knot until they've been taught by someone like me.

say: I'd tell the library to run more **classes** and the council to make a local plan.
I'd say find what you like doing with **hands or people** and get good at it.
think: I feel **okay**, since I'd still be fit at sixty-nine with time to save.
The hard part is the **pension** staying at 1,300 while prices creep up.
do: Fix the **roof** in the first year with a small loan and savings.
Take on a young **apprentice** in the shed workshop.
Keep learning the next **AI tools** and the repair café.
feel: It feels like a brisk **puzzle**, and I'd rather know what's coming.
S3.quote: The machines can write the invoice, but they can't tell you which board has a hidden knot until they've been taught by someone like me.
fieldNote: Five years brings an **apprentice** plan, which passes on her craft.
Eager for the next tools, not afraid of them.
The pension is the only fragile point.

steps.text: Fix the roof within a year using a small loan
Take on a young apprentice in the shed workshop
Try each new AI design tool as it appears
Keep running the repair café on Wednesdays and Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say we're lucky, and let's do it properly. I'd be vocal about a dividend for everybody, because if the machines do the work, we all fed them the knowledge. I'd say it at the market stall and online. A decade is enough time to write good rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel calm, to tell the truth. I'd be seventy-four by then, and the tools will have changed everything I know. But I'd keep up, I always have. The worry is the same, a small pension, so I'd get my money in order early, and keep saying my piece to the politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fix the roof this year, set up a small pot of savings, 20 a week, and build a proper workshop with an apprentice. I'd teach the AI class at the library, and expand it to a repair-and-learn day. And I'd travel a bit while my knees are good, maybe a trip to the coast with Imogen and her son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels distant and kind of exciting. A bit like watching a ship being built. I'd be nervous, yes, but I'd also want to see it finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is the longest warning. What do you do with it that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I could still earn from the craft, maybe through teaching the younger ones. By the time AGI arrives, I might be ready to retire for real. If the world gets cheaper and the dividend arrives, I'd be better off than now. If not, I'd have my tables and my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a dividend, if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my daughter asked, I'd say don't panic. Teach if you like teaching, but pick up a second skill that involves hands or people. And look after your pension as if it were a garden, because nobody else will.

say: I'd say we're **lucky** to have ten years and should write good rules properly.
I'd say a **dividend** for everybody is fair, since we all fed the machines.
think: I feel **calm**, because I've always kept up with new tools.
My one worry is the same: a **small pension**.
do: Fix the **roof** this year and save 20 a week.
Teach the library **AI class** and turn it into a repair-and-learn day.
Take a **trip** to the coast with my daughter and her son while my knees are good.
feel: It feels **distant** and exciting, like watching a ship being built.
S4.quote: Look after your pension as if it were a garden, because nobody else will.
fieldNote: The longest warning gives **calm**, but not full security because of the thin pension.
Plans a trip and teaching, so she's turning change into a life she wants.
Speaks of the dividend as a matter of fairness.

steps.text: Fix the roof this year and save 20 a week
Build a proper workshop in the shed with an apprentice
Grow the library class into a repair-and-learn day
Take a coast trip with my daughter and her son

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I haven't fixed the roof and the money isn't there. What would help is a simple dividend or a pension that follows prices, a roof grant for older owners, and free classes so nobody older is left out. And the library staying open, that's where I find my people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that older people aren't as stuck as everyone thinks. I'm sixty-four, I use an AI helper every day, and I'm making tables from old oak. Ask older people, don't assume. And if you think we're slow, come and watch me fix a toaster in four minutes with a chatbot reading me the diagram.

headlineQuote: Ask older people, don't assume. And if you think we're slow, come and watch me fix a toaster in four minutes with a chatbot reading me the diagram.
portrait: Zoe is **64**, a retired joiner living alone in a small flat she owns, and she uses an AI helper every day.
She runs the **repair café**, sells tables at a market and wants a dividend from machine profits.
She sees **opportunity** in the tools because her craft is hands-on.
Her one steady pressure is a **thin pension** and a roof that needs doing.
biggestWorry: Two years worries her most, because she hasn't fixed the **roof** and has no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A simple **dividend** or price-linked pension, a roof grant for older owners and free classes.
